parts:
Hi, 

I think I got the problem solved. I inspected the code more by going through step by step what is generated in different stages. The problem was really because of only one variant being called for the chromosome.

In

finalcall=finalcall[-1,]

the first row in finalcall matrix (containing the results) containing only NAs is removed. In the case of 0 or 2 or more variants, the matrix stays as matrix. But when only one variant would be called, this step changes the finalcall matrix into "value" for some reason. I solved this by forcing the matrix by adding

finalcall=(as.matrix(finalcall[-1,]))

which gives a matrix with rows and columns inverted, but I'm working on from here... Thanks for advice.

I'd still like to know if I have the permission to use this targeted exome sequencing analysis CODEX version in my master's thesis.

Best regards,
Salla

parts:
Hi,

Thanks for your interest in CODEX. If I understand correctly, you have targeted sequencing with large targets capturing large segments of the genome covering multiple genes. In this case, you should definitely separate the large segments to consecutive NON-OVERLAPPING bins (1Kb recommended). Or you can get the exonic regions of the genes instead and use those as bins.

Each line in the input .bed file should be a non-overlapping target. In your case, it cannot be a large chunk 10752 - 66487 since the segmentation by CODEX has the resolution of a target (i.e., CODEX doesn’t segment within a target but instead either include or not include the entire target in the CNV region). For targeted sequencing, since the targets are usually very sparse in the entire genome and thus the segmentation is carried out within each gene by CODEX. You should include a fourth column in the .bed file indicating the gene information for the corresponding target. With this said, if you want these pseudogenes to be segmented altogether, you should have the same name for them; if you want the segment to be carried out within each pseudogene, you should name them differently.

Hope that this clarifies,
Yuchao

Hi,

You are right in that almost all kb targets got filtered out due to extreme coverage. I think there must be something that you miss here. If I understand correctly, you are using targeted sequencing. Yuchao

Calls: cbind -> standardGeneric -> eval -> eval -> eval -> .Method

On Wednesday, March 8, 2017 at 11:32:09 AM UTC-5, Yuchao Jiang wrote:
Hi,

Thanks for your interest in CODEX. If I understand correctly, you have targeted sequencing with large targets capturing large segments of the genome covering multiple genes. In this case, you should definitely separate the large segments to consecutive NON-OVERLAPPING bins (1Kb recommended). Or you can get the exonic regions of the genes instead and use those as bins.

Each line in the input .bed file should be a non-overlapping target. In your case, it cannot be a large chunk 10752 - 66487 since the segmentation by CODEX has the resolution of a target (i.e., CODEX doesn’t segment within a target but instead either include or not include the entire target in the CNV region). For targeted sequencing, since the targets are usually very sparse in the entire genome and thus the segmentation is carried out within each gene by CODEX. You should include a fourth column in the .bed file indicating the gene information for the corresponding target. With this said, if you want these pseudogenes to be segmented altogether, you should have the same name for them; if you want the segment to be carried out within each pseudogene, you should name them differently.

Hope that this clarifies,
Yuchao

This error is not unexpected. CODEX uses an iterative algorithm to estimate the parameters and more specifically, within each iteration, CODEX uses Poisson glm to get the hidden Poisson factors. With this said, if the number of latent factors (aka, K) is set greater than 10, the Poisson glm (default function in R) fails to converge and this leads to the error.

You can refer to the output pdf (AIC, BIC, and residual variance) to determine the optimal K but once again, since you are using normalize2() which uses only the normal samples to estimate the exon-wise factors, the choice shouldn't affect your results too much around the optimum.

Hope that this clarifies,

If I remember correctly, your sequencing platform was targeted sequencing? If you follow the segmentation code for targeted sequencing, the segmentation should be conducted within each gene. With this said, sometimes we also observed some samples behaving very weirdly, e.g., some regions contains consecutive deletions and duplications, in a similar fashion to chromothripsis. However we are not sure whether they are true and usually filter these samples out. So one possible explanation is that the data quality isn't good or the data are from multiple sources, batches etc, in which case the cross-sample normalization step doesn't really help much.

Another possibility is the QC procedure. From the 1000 Genomes Project whole-exome data, which is of high quality from our perspective, we also observe regions where a lot of the samples contain either deletions or duplications. It turns out that these regions overlap with segmental duplication regions or regions that are hard to map. So one way to filter is to exclude CNVs that overlap with seg duplication regions.

One of our collaborators found that there were a lot of short CNVs being called (short as in number of exons). They found that filtering out all CNVs containing 2 exons or 3 exons removes a lot of the calls that are more likely to be false positives.

Hope that this helps you.

I thought your data was from targeted sequencing. CODEX is designed for exome sequencing and is further adapted to targeted sequencing. The latter has per-gene segmentation (i.e. CODEX perform segmentation within each gene for targeted sequencing since the targets are too sparse and it doesn't make sense to perform segmentation on an entire chromosome).

No those CNV calls encompass 25%-75% of the chromosome thus are multi-allelic. I did also notice some intervals in my results that read in descending chromosomal position (i.e chrN:50000-35000) which seemed odd to me.

The current result you have:  large dups/dels > 25Mb within ONE gene? The segmentation by CODEX for targeted sequencing is done within each gene due to the sparsity of the targets in the genome.

On Tue, Mar 28, 2017 at 2:56 PM, <n.b....@gmail.com> wrote:
I actually ended up narrowing my bed file to contain only exons from a panel of 76 genes of interest for my first run of the codex analysis. I have the intention of comparing results from a few different bed files to optimize the protocol including an original bed file that more closely overlaps the bait intervals and another approach containing extremely large targets that have been broken down into evenly sized smaller targets. I am not sure if I obtained some questionable results (a number of extremely large dups/dels > 25Mb as well as some CNVs that appear to be called for a high percentage of the ~100 samples I am working with) because my exon exclusive bed file is simply too sparse a dataset for a targeted sequencing analysis via codex. Unfortunately I am currently sitting in a long queue for computing resources and probably won't be able to run codex with the other bed files for a while, so I am trying to make the best sense of the results I already have. I certainly appreciate your prompt responses and patience with my requests as I become more familiar with your software!

On Monday, March 27, 2017 at 10:29:34 PM UTC-4, Yuchao Jiang wrote:
If I remember correctly, your sequencing platform was targeted sequencing? If you follow the segmentation code for targeted sequencing, the segmentation should be conducted within each gene. With this said, sometimes we also observed some samples behaving very weirdly, e.g., some regions contains consecutive deletions and duplications, in a similar fashion to chromothripsis. However we are not sure whether they are true and usually filter these samples out. So one possible explanation is that the data quality isn't good or the data are from multiple sources, batches etc, in which case the cross-sample normalization step doesn't really help much.

Another possibility is the QC procedure. From the 1000 Genomes Project whole-exome data, which is of high quality from our perspective, we also observe regions where a lot of the samples contain either deletions or duplications. It turns out that these regions overlap with segmental duplication regions or regions that are hard to map. So one way to filter is to exclude CNVs that overlap with seg duplication regions.

One of our collaborators found that there were a lot of short CNVs being called (short as in number of exons). They found that filtering out all CNVs containing 2 exons or 3 exons removes a lot of the calls that are more likely to be false positives.

Hope that this helps you.

Hi,

If the additional samples you added were from different sequencing batches, from our experience, this doesn’t help with previous normalization. It would be good to have some positive and negative controls or view the calling results as a sanity check in this case.

Hope that this helps,
Yuchao

Thank you very much! I was able to finish running the program and successfully called at least one of my positive controls. I ended up selecting a new bed file which contains only exonic regions for a panel of genes I am interested in. If I have more sequencing data available, would you recommend incorporating as much data into Codex as possible for stronger normalization? As my knowledge of your actual algorithm is limited, I don't want to assume a "more is better" approach supersedes specificity in terms of number of targets used for normalization and codex's ability to accurately call cnvs.

On Thursday, March 23, 2017 at 2:22:58 PM UTC-4, Yuchao Jiang wrote:
This error is not unexpected. CODEX uses an iterative algorithm to estimate the parameters and more specifically, within each iteration, CODEX uses Poisson glm to get the hidden Poisson factors. With this said, if the number of latent factors (aka, K) is set greater than 10, the Poisson glm (default function in R) fails to converge and this leads to the error.

We seldom set the range of K to exceed 10, especially if you use the normalize2() function. Just set K=1:10 for the normalization step. You can refer to the output pdf (AIC, BIC, and residual variance) to determine the optimal K but once again, since you are using normalize2() which uses only the normal samples to estimate the exon-wise factors, the choice shouldn't affect your results too much around the optimum.

Hope that this clarifies,
Yuchao

Hi,

Thanks for your interest in CODEX. If I understand correctly, you have targeted sequencing with large targets capturing large segments of the genome covering multiple genes. In this case, you should definitely separate the large segments to consecutive NON-OVERLAPPING bins (1Kb recommended). Or you can get the exonic regions of the genes instead and use those as bins.

Each line in the input .bed file should be a non-overlapping target. In your case, it cannot be a large chunk 10752 - 66487 since the segmentation by CODEX has the resolution of a target (i.e., CODEX doesn’t segment within a target but instead either include or not include the entire target in the CNV region). For targeted sequencing, since the targets are usually very sparse in the entire genome and thus the segmentation is carried out within each gene by CODEX. You should include a fourth column in the .bed file indicating the gene information for the corresponding target. With this said, if you want these pseudogenes to be segmented altogether, you should have the same name for them; if you want the segment to be carried out within each pseudogene, you should name them differently.

Hope that this clarifies,
Yuchao

Without looking at your data, I am here listing a few possible explanations and hopefully they can be of help:

1) batch effect as you mentioned. Mostly likely your samples are from multiple batches since you have 600 of them. To do this, we recommend separating the sample pool into different batches and process them separately. You can try increasing K but with a larger K it takes longer to run and can lead to possible convergence errors. I recently added a few common questions on this topic on our github page -- please check it out if this is not clear.

2. Those are from segmental duplication regions and thus you probably want to zoom into the region by loading it into UCSC browser for example.

3. Those are real common CNV signals. Your positive controls won't necessarily have the highest likelihood. The Poisson likelihood ratio of alternative versus null can be large by a long cnv event, a large copy number change, or a high depth of coverage.

Yuchao

On Thursday, March 23, 2017 at 2:22:58 PM UTC-4, Yuchao Jiang wrote:
This error is not unexpected. CODEX uses an iterative algorithm to estimate the parameters and more specifically, within each iteration, CODEX uses Poisson glm to get the hidden Poisson factors. With this said, if the number of latent factors (aka, K) is set greater than 10, the Poisson glm (default function in R) fails to converge and this leads to the error.

We seldom set the range of K to exceed 10, especially if you use the normalize2() function. Just set K=1:10 for the normalization step. You can refer to the output pdf (AIC, BIC, and residual variance) to determine the optimal K but once again, since you are using normalize2() which uses only the normal samples to estimate the exon-wise factors, the choice shouldn't affect your results too much around the optimum.

Hope that this clarifies,
Yuchao
